term.name: Crib (probable word)
term.short: A crib is a guessed plaintext fragment used to test positions, keys, or structure in a ciphertext.
term.meta_description: Learn how probable words and phrases help test ciphertext alignments and keys, why a crib is a hypothesis rather than known plaintext, and when it fails.

body.title: Definition
body.html: A crib is a word, phrase, header, or pattern suspected to occur in the plaintext. The analyst aligns it with ciphertext positions and checks whether the implied key or transformation remains consistent elsewhere.

body.title: Choosing a crib
body.html: Greetings, dates, protocol markers, file signatures, repeated formats, and topic-specific vocabulary provide candidates. A crib is not confirmed known plaintext; it becomes useful only when independent evidence supports the alignment.

body.title: Applications and limits
body.html: Cribs helped attack classical machines and reused one-time-pad keystreams. A wrong guess creates false leads, and secure modern encryption prevents local plaintext guesses from revealing corresponding key material.

faq.question: Is a crib known plaintext?
faq.answer: No. It is probable plaintext until verified.

faq.question: What is crib dragging?
faq.answer: It slides a guessed fragment across related ciphertexts, testing where the resulting text looks plausible.

faq.question: Can any common word serve as a crib?
faq.answer: It can be tried, but context-specific and structurally constrained guesses are much stronger.
